name: The Use Theory of Meaning
statement: Don't ask what a word stands for; ask how it is used in the life of the language.
statementAccent: how it is used in the life of the language
meaning: The use theory of meaning is the later Ludwig Wittgenstein's conception of meaning, developed in the Philosophical Investigations of 1953, on which the meaning of a word or expression is not an object it stands for, nor a mental idea or image associated with it, but its use in the language, how it is actually employed in the practice of a linguistic community. Wittgenstein put the point in a famous remark, often cited as section 43, that for a large class of cases, though not for all, in which we employ the word meaning, it can be defined thus: the meaning of a word is its use in the language. The deliberate qualification, though not for all, marks this as a characteristic emphasis and rule of thumb rather than a rigid universal theory. To understand meaning, Wittgenstein directs us to look at the many diverse activities in which language is interwoven with action, which he calls language-games, from giving orders and describing to joking, requesting, and thanking, illustrated by the simple builders language-game. These language-games are embedded in shared human forms of life, so that, as he puts it, to imagine a language is to imagine a form of life. Wittgenstein also introduced family resemblance to explain that the things a word covers need share no single defining essence, only a network of overlapping similarities, as with the word game. The use theory rejects the referential, so-called Augustinian, picture on which every word is a name standing for an object.
mechanism: The use theory replaces the search for an object or idea that a word stands for with attention to how the word functions in practice. On the referential picture Wittgenstein criticizes, associated with a passage from Augustine that opens the Investigations, every word is a name that means by standing for an object, and a sentence is a combination of such names. Wittgenstein argues that this picture, which his own earlier work had partly embodied, distorts how language actually works, since a vast range of expressions do not name anything, and even for those that do, knowing the object is not the same as knowing the meaning. Instead, he says, we should look at the use, at the role a word plays in the various language-games in which it figures. A language-game is a rule-governed activity in which speaking is woven together with doing, such as the builders game in which calling out slab is part of an activity of building. Because meaning is use, it is grounded not in private mental accompaniments but in public, shared practices and customs, the forms of life in which language-games are embedded. The notion of family resemblance completes the picture: seeking the common essence that all games, or all instances of any general term, must share is a mistake, for we find instead a complicated network of similarities overlapping and criss-crossing, family resemblances, that hold the applications of a word together without any single defining feature. Understanding a word, then, is mastering its use, being able to go on employing it correctly within the relevant practice.

examples.text: For a large class of cases, Wittgenstein said, the meaning of a word is its use in the language, not an object it names.
Language is woven into activities like ordering, describing, and joking, so meaning is grasped through the language-game a word plays in.
Games share no single defining feature, only a network of overlapping similarities, so word use need not rest on a common essence.

variants.name: Language-games and forms of life
variants.text: Meaning grasped through the rule-governed activities of language, embedded in shared human forms of life.

variants.name: Family resemblance
variants.text: The rejection of shared essences: a word's applications are held together by overlapping similarities, not one common feature.

whyItMatters: The use theory of meaning is one of the most influential ideas in twentieth-century philosophy, marking the later Wittgenstein's break with the referential picture of language and, indeed, with his own early work. By insisting that meaning is a matter of use in a public practice rather than of naming objects or entertaining private ideas, Wittgenstein reoriented the philosophy of language away from the search for the entities words stand for and toward the study of how language actually functions in human life. His notions of language-games, forms of life, and family resemblance became part of the common vocabulary of philosophy and beyond, reshaping debates about meaning, understanding, rule-following, and the nature of concepts, and undermining the assumption that every meaningful general term must correspond to a shared essence. The use theory helped inspire ordinary language philosophy and fed into pragmatics and later use-based and inferentialist accounts of meaning, which locate content in the role expressions play in inference and communication rather than in word-world correspondence. It also connects to Wittgenstein's private language argument, since meaning as public use leaves no room for a purely private language. As the view that to know a word's meaning is to know its use, it is a landmark in the study of language.

working.text: stop asking what object or idea a word stands for and reject the picture that every word is a name.
examine how the word is actually employed in the language-games and practices where it figures.
allow that the word's applications may share no essence, only overlapping similarities, and are grounded in a form of life.

limits: The use theory is enormously influential but faces questions of precision and scope. Wittgenstein himself hedged the slogan, saying meaning is use only for a large class of cases, though not for all, and did not offer it as a rigorous, general definition, so treating meaning is use as a complete, precise theory overstates his claim; critics complain that the notion of use is itself vague and that not everything one does with a word is part of its meaning. It is contested how far the approach can be systematized into a workable semantics, and later use-based and inferentialist theories that draw on Wittgenstein have had to add much apparatus he did not supply. There are also hard questions about how public use fixes correctness without collapsing into whatever the community happens to do, questions that surface in the rule-following debate. Precise section numbers and quotations, such as the meaning-is-use remark at section 43, the builders game at section 2, and the family resemblance discussion at sections 66 to 67, and the exact wording of translations, reward care. So the use theory robustly relocates meaning in public use, understood as a profound but deliberately non-systematic emphasis whose central notion of use invites further precision.
misreadings: The use theory is not the claim that meaning is whatever any individual does with a word; use is public and rule-governed, embedded in shared practice. Wittgenstein did not offer meaning is use as a rigid universal definition, since he restricted it to a large class of cases though not all. And rejecting shared essences via family resemblance does not make word use arbitrary, only that it need not rest on a single common feature, so treating meaning as private idiosyncratic use, as a strict universal theory, or as making concepts arbitrary, misreads the later Wittgenstein.
origin: The later Ludwig Wittgenstein's conception, in the Philosophical Investigations (1953), that the meaning of a word is its use in the language, developed through the notions of language-games, forms of life, and family resemblance.
